pages.summary: Binds the SDK hook event roster, matcher rules, output shape and per-event timeout defaults. Our plugin hook runtime covers all of it except one event that exists only on this page: DirectoryAdded.

findings.claim: The SDK hook roster includes a DirectoryAdded event that fires when a working directory is added mid-session; it is absent from hooks.md's own table, so this page is the only place it is specified.
findings.quote: | `DirectoryAdded`                                       | No         | Yes            | A working directory is added during a session                                                                                          | Install dependencies for a repository added mid-session                                                     |
findings.ourState: `DirectoryAdded` does not exist anywhere in the repo (`grep -ran DirectoryAdded packages apps docs scripts` → 0). `PluginHookEventName` enumerates 30 names and its own doc comment accounts for exactly two documented events as deliberate deferrals (`MessageDisplay`, `TeammateIdle`) — DirectoryAdded is unaccounted for. The surface it would fire on does exist: we ship session-scoped `addDirectories` grants (`pi-agent.ts:3189`).
findings.evidence: packages/shared/src/plugins/hooks-runtime.ts:25 (union), :156 (PLUGIN_HOOK_EVENTS list); grep -ran "DirectoryAdded" packages apps docs scripts → 0 hits

pages.summary: The configuration schema, matcher rules, exit-code table, timeout defaults, decision-control shapes and the 8-block Stop cap all match. The divergences are all in per-event payload FIELD NAMES that our emitters spell differently, plus several documented input/output fields with no producer at all — a hook script reading the documented key gets nothing.

findings.claim: Setup hooks receive a `trigger` field whose value is `init` or `maintenance`.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), Setup hooks receive a `trigger` field set to either `"init"` or `"maintenance"`:
findings.ourState: Our Setup emission carries `source: 'pi-runtime'` and no `trigger` at all, and it fires on every Pi session start rather than only under `--init-only` / `-p --init` / `-p --maintenance`.

findings.claim: FileChanged input carries `file_path` (absolute path) and `event` (`change` | `add` | `unlink`).
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), FileChanged hooks receive `file_path` and `event`.
findings.ourState: We emit `path` (only when a path was captured) and `change_kind` set to the mutating TOOL NAME, never `file_path` or `event`. The stdin payload is the event input verbatim (`hookCommandStdinPayload` spreads `...input`), so a hook doing `jq -r .file_path` reads null.

findings.claim: CwdChanged input carries `old_cwd` and `new_cwd`.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), CwdChanged hooks receive `old_cwd` and `new_cwd`.
findings.ourState: We emit `cwd` and `previous_cwd`. Neither documented key is produced anywhere (`grep -ran 'old_cwd\|new_cwd' packages apps` → 0 outside docs).

findings.claim: StopFailure input carries `error`, and that field is what the matcher filters on.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), StopFailure hooks receive `error`, optional `error_details`, and optional `last_assistant_message`. The `error` field identifies the error type and is used for matcher filtering.
findings.ourState: We emit `error_code` only. The MATCHER path was fixed (`getMatchValueForSdkInput` reads `input.error_code ?? input.error` and maps it through `STOP_FAILURE_DOCUMENTED_ERROR`), but the payload a hook reads on stdin still has no `error` key, and `error_details` / `last_assistant_message` have no producer.

findings.claim: ConfigChange input carries `source` (the configuration type that changed) and optionally `file_path`.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), ConfigChange hooks receive `source` and optionally `file_path`. The `source` field indicates which configuration type changed, and `file_path` provides the path to the specific file that was modified.
findings.ourState: We emit `config_keys` and `config_digest`; neither `source` nor `file_path` is produced, so the documented matcher vocabulary (`user_settings`, `project_settings`, `local_settings`, `policy_settings`, `skills`) can never match — `getMatchValueForSdkInput` deliberately leaves ConfigChange unmatched for that reason.

findings.claim: UserPromptExpansion input carries `expansion_type`, `command_name`, `command_args`, `command_source` and the original `prompt`, and the matcher filters on `command_name`.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), UserPromptExpansion hooks receive `expansion_type`, `command_name`, `command_args`, `command_source`, and the original `prompt` string.
findings.ourState: Our UserPromptExpansion emission carries only `source: 'pi-before-agent-start'`, `lifecycle_version` and `correlation_id`, and fires once per turn rather than per command expansion. None of the five documented fields has a producer (`grep -ran expansion_type packages apps` → 0).

findings.claim: PreCompact input carries `custom_instructions`; PostCompact input carries `compact_summary`.
findings.quote: In addition to the [common input fields](#common-input-fields), PostCompact hooks receive `trigger` and `compact_summary`. The `compact_summary` field contains the conversation summary generated by the compact operation.
findings.ourState: Both emissions carry `trigger` and a Nessy `source` only. `compact_summary` and `custom_instructions` have no producer anywhere in the repo.

findings.claim: `prompt_id` is a common input field on every hook event, correlating hook output with OpenTelemetry `prompt.id`.
findings.quote: | `prompt_id`       | UUID identifying the user prompt currently being processed.
findings.ourState: `SdkAutomationInput` has no `prompt_id` field and no emitter sets one (`grep -ran 'prompt_id\|promptId' packages apps --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx` → 0).

findings.claim: `effort` is a common input field (an object with a `level` field) on tool-context events, and the same value reaches hook commands as `$CLAUDE_EFFORT`.
findings.quote: The level is also available to hook commands and the Bash tool as the `$CLAUDE_EFFORT` environment variable.
findings.ourState: `SdkAutomationInput` has no `effort` field, and `buildHookCommandEnv` sets `NESSY_EVENT`, `NESSY_EVENT_DATA`, six inherited keys and thirteen `NESSY_*` field mirrors — no effort variable in either spelling. (`${CLAUDE_EFFORT}` IS substituted for skills, `runtime-skill-content.ts:136`, so the value exists; it just never reaches a hook.)

findings.claim: SessionStart hooks can return four event-specific output fields: `initialUserMessage`, `sessionTitle`, `watchPaths` and `reloadSkills`.
findings.quote: | `reloadSkills`       | Boolean. When `true`, Claude Code re-scans the [skill](/docs/en/skills) and command directories after the SessionStart hooks complete, so skills the hook installed are available in the same session, starting with the first prompt
findings.ourState: None of the four is read. `grep -ran 'reloadSkills\|initialUserMessage\|watchPaths' packages apps --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx` → 0 in source (only unrelated dist bundles); `sessionTitle` appears only as an unrelated React prop in `apps/viewer`. The parsed hook-output decision type carries none of them.

findings.claim: UserPromptSubmit output accepts `suppressOriginalPrompt`, which omits the original prompt text from the block message when `decision` is `"block"`.
findings.quote: | `suppressOriginalPrompt` | If `true` when `decision` is `"block"`, omits the original prompt text from the block message shown to the user        |
findings.ourState: No reader: `grep -ran suppressOriginalPrompt packages apps` → 0 (the only hit in the repo is a note in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-26-r-queue-doc-verification.md:462).

pages.summary: Restates the hooks.md contract (event table, exit codes, matcher fields, `if` semantics, decision precedence) — all of which we match; the divergences it shares with hooks.md are filed there. One binding is unique to this page: the env override for the Stop-hook block cap.

findings.claim: The 8-consecutive-block Stop cap can be raised with an environment variable.
findings.quote: If your hook legitimately needs more than eight iterations to converge, raise the cap with [`CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`](/docs/en/env-vars).
findings.ourState: The cap is a hardcoded module constant with no environment override in any spelling (`grep -ran 'STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP' packages apps` → 0): `const MAX_CONSECUTIVE_HOOK_BLOCKS = 8;`.

pages.summary: The six-step evaluation order (hooks → deny → ask → mode → allow → canUseTool), the six mode names and their semantics, bare-name-deny tool removal, deny-side tool-name globs, the allow-glob anchoring rule, and Edit-governs-all-writers are each implemented and cited in-code. The `canUseTool` shadowing warning (`CLAUDE_SDK_CAN_USE_TOOL_SHADOWED`) is an SDK-embedder diagnostic with no Nessy counterpart surface.

Mode vocabulary, strictness order, subagent clamp, the protected-path directory/file lists and the bypass/dontAsk outcomes all match verbatim. The protected-path per-mode table has grown two rows we do not implement.

findings.claim: In plan mode, a protected-path write is allowed when bypass permissions are available for the session, and routed to the classifier when auto mode is available during planning — not simply prompted.
findings.quote: | `plan`                   | Prompted. {/* min-version: 2.1.217 */}In sessions with [bypass permissions](#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) available, allowed. {/* min-version: 2.1.218 */}Otherwise, with [auto mode](#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) available during planning, routed to the classifier |
findings.ourState: `protectedPathOutcome` is a three-branch total function keyed on mode alone: `bypassPermissions` → allow, `dontAsk` → deny, everything else → prompt. It has no notion of "bypass available" or of auto-during-plan, and the file's own quoted copy of the table predates both rows. (The `auto` row's classifier routing is a separately recorded deliberate deviation documented in the same file.)

pages.summary: Rule syntax, deny/ask/allow precedence, parameter rules, wrapper stripping, the four path anchors, gitignore depth semantics, WebFetch domain matching, Agent and Cd rules, and the EndConversation carve-out are all implemented and cited. Divergences: a specifier'd whole-tool deny does not remove the tool from context, `Skill(...)` rules are inert, and several managed-only keys have no reader.

findings.claim: `Bash(*)` is equivalent to a bare `Bash`, and as a deny rule BOTH forms remove the tool from Claude's context.
findings.quote: `Bash(*)` is equivalent to `Bash` and matches all Bash commands. As a deny rule, both forms remove the tool from Claude's context.
findings.ourState: `Bash(*)` parses to `{ kind: 'bash', pattern: '*' }` — a pattern matcher, not a tool matcher. Context removal is decided by `isWholeCapabilityDeniedByPermissionDsl`, which only inspects `rule.matcher.kind === 'tool'`, so a `deny: ["Bash(*)"]` leaves the Bash tool definition in the model's context and denies every call it makes instead of hiding the tool. Same for `PowerShell(*)`.

findings.claim: `Skill(<name pattern>)` is a supported rule format that matches by skill name.
findings.quote: | `Skill(deploy *)`              | Skill                     | [Skill name matching](/docs/en/skills#restrict-claude’s-skill-access) |
findings.ourState: `parseClaudeRuleString` has no `Skill` case; `Skill(deploy *)` contains no `param:` colon, so it falls through to the `default:` branch and returns an inert warning ("uses a specifier form no permission check matches; the rule is ignored"). There is no `skill` matcher kind in `CompiledMatcher`, so an imported Claude `deny: ["Skill(deploy *)"]` silently grants the skill.

findings.claim: `blockedMarketplaces` is a managed-only setting: a blocklist of marketplace sources checked before download.
findings.quote: | `blockedMarketplaces`                          | Blocklist of marketplace sources. Blocked sources are checked before downloading, so they never touch the filesystem.
findings.ourState: No reader (`grep -ran blockedMarketplaces packages apps` → 0). `ManagedPiPolicyV1` implements the sibling keys `strictKnownMarketplaces` and `extraKnownMarketplaces` but has no denylist field, so an admin can pin an allowlist but cannot block a single source.
findings.evidence: packages/shared/src/agent/pi-harness/managed-policy.ts:141,158 (the two marketplace fields that do exist)

findings.claim: `strictPluginOnlyCustomization` is a managed-only setting that blocks skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers from user and project sources; it accepts `true` or an array naming a subset.
findings.quote: | `strictPluginOnlyCustomization`                | Block skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers from user and project sources, so they can only come from plugins or managed settings. `true` locks all four surfaces; an array such as `["skills", "hooks"]` locks only the named ones.
findings.ourState: No reader (`grep -ran strictPluginOnlyCustomization packages apps` → 0). We implement the per-surface locks `allowManagedHooksOnly`, `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` and `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, but nothing locks user/project SKILLS or AGENTS to plugin-or-managed origin.

findings.claim: With sandboxing enabled, `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` defaults to `true` and makes sandboxed Bash commands run without prompting even against a bare `Bash` ask rule.
findings.quote: When you enable sandboxing and leave `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` at its default of `true`, sandboxed Bash commands run without prompting even if your permissions include a bare `Bash` ask rule, or the [equivalent `Bash(*)` form](#match-all-uses-of-a-tool): the sandbox boundary substitutes for that whole-tool prompt.
findings.ourState: The key has no reader (`grep -ran autoAllowBashIfSandboxed packages apps` → 0) and does not appear in our sandbox settings schema, which carries only `excludedCommands`, the four filesystem root lists and the two domain lists.

findings.claim: `disableSideloadFlags` and `pluginTrustMessage` are managed-only settings governing CLI sideload flags and the plugin trust warning.
findings.quote: | `pluginTrustMessage`                           | Custom message appended to the plugin trust warning shown before installation
findings.ourState: Neither key has a reader (`grep -ran 'disableSideloadFlags\|pluginTrustMessage' packages apps` → 0), and neither appears in `ManagedPiPolicyV1`. We do ship plugin install with a trust step and marketplace pinning, so both bind a surface we have.

pages.summary: The page primarily binds the Agent SDK's tool-authoring API (`tool()`, `createSdkMcpServer`), which Nessy does not expose. What does bind us is the MCP result contract it specifies — tool name format, content-block types, `isError`, and `structuredContent` — and our MCP proxy drops two of the five documented block types.

findings.claim: A tool result's `content` array may carry `resource` and `resource_link` blocks in addition to text/image/audio, and the runtime converts a resource link into a text block naming the link.
findings.quote: The `content` array in a tool result accepts `text`, `image`, `audio`, `resource`, and `resource_link` blocks. You can mix them in the same response.
findings.ourState: The MCP proxy's result reducer handles exactly `text`, `image` and `audio`. A `resource` block's payload (`resource.text` / `resource.blob`, the actual content) and a `resource_link` block are both skipped by the loop, so in any result that also contains a text block the resource content is silently lost — the `JSON.stringify(result)` fallback only fires when zero parts were extracted.

findings.claim: When `structuredContent` is set on a tool result, text blocks in `content` are not forwarded to the model.
findings.quote: When `structuredContent` is set, Claude receives the JSON plus any image or resource blocks from `content`. Text blocks in `content` are not forwarded, since they are assumed to duplicate the structured data.
findings.ourState: We always join every text block into `text` and return it alongside `structuredContent`; there is no branch that suppresses text blocks when structured content is present, so an MCP server following the documented pattern sends the same data twice.

pages.summary: We implement a client-side equivalent (`mcp__tool_search` / `mcp__tool_load` plus a host catalog) rather than the API beta, and the env override parses every documented value. The unset default differs, which the code records as a deliberate deviation.

findings.claim: With the variable unset, tool search is ON: definitions are deferred and discovered on demand, with no count or percentage consulted. The 10% threshold belongs only to the opt-in `auto` value.
findings.quote: | (unset)  | Tool search is on. Tool definitions are deferred and discovered on demand. Falls back to loading upfront on Google Cloud's Agent Platform, a non-first-party `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, or a Microsoft Foundry deployment hosted on Azure.
findings.ourState: Our unset case (`kind: 'default'`) defers only when BOTH a workspace preference is on AND the deferrable candidate count exceeds a threshold (48 by default); otherwise every definition loads upfront. `always`/`never`/`auto`/`auto:N` match the page. The file documents this as a deliberate deviation, including that the Nessy Gateway is a non-first-party host on Claude's own rules.

findings.claim: A search returns up to five most relevant tools per search by default, and the catalog is capped at 10,000 tools.
findings.quote: * **Search results:** returns up to five most relevant tools per search by default
findings.ourState: `mcp__tool_search` defaults `limit` to 20 (clamped 1..50), and the capability catalog has no maximum-entry cap — only a 32 KiB output byte budget.

pages.summary: Tool names are declared to be the exact strings used in permission rules, subagent tool lists and hook matchers, and our binding table honours that verbatim for EnterWorktree/ExitWorktree/ReportFindings/PushNotification/SendUserFile/Cron*/Monitor/NotebookEdit/WebFetch/WebSearch. One canonical name is spelled differently on the permission axis, and the Skill rule format (filed under permissions.md) also originates here.

findings.claim: The canonical tool name is `TaskStop`; permission rules and hook matchers match the canonical name only, and the transcript label `Stop Task` does not match.
findings.quote: For example, the tool labeled `Stop Task` in the transcript has the canonical name `TaskStop`. Permission rules and [hook matchers](/docs/en/hooks) match the canonical name only, so a rule written as `Stop Task` doesn't match.
findings.ourState: The binding spells it `stopTask` on every permission-visible axis — `binding('stop_task', 'stop_task', 'stopTask', 'stopTask')` gives semanticId `stop_task`, permissionName/bindingName `stopTask`. `PERMISSION_RULE_TOOL_NAMES` is derived from permissionName+descriptorId, so `TaskStop` is not a known tool: an imported `deny: ["TaskStop"]` matches nothing AND raises the unknown-tool typo warning. A `taskstop` alias exists only for SUBAGENT tool lists (`runtime-agent-definition.ts:95`), not for permission rules or hook matchers.

pages.summary: The page binds Anthropic-hosted delivery of managed settings from the claude.ai admin console over api.anthropic.com — a platform Nessy does not ship (and which the page itself says is unavailable behind a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, i.e. our gateway). The parts that bind a surface we DO ship — tolerant salvage of invalid managed entries, `forceRemoteSettingsRefresh`, and ConfigChange-based auditing — are implemented; the managed-only keys with no reader are filed under permissions.md.

findings.claim: A delivered payload with an entry that fails schema validation is salvaged: the bad entry is stripped, a validation error surfaced, and every remaining valid setting applied.
findings.quote: When a payload contains an entry that fails schema validation, Claude Code strips that entry, surfaces a validation error, and applies every remaining valid setting.
findings.ourState: Implemented, with the same polarity choices recorded per field — `tolerate`/`securitySwitch` strip or tighten each key and record a typed drop that `nessy-general-agent doctor` prints. `forceRemoteSettingsRefresh` is also carried (`managed-policy.ts:385`). Listed here as the page's one binding claim that we do satisfy; no divergence.

pages.summary: Binds the whole settings key surface, precedence, sandbox key schema, worktree keys and plugin/marketplace settings. We implement a large subset, but the sandbox filesystem keys are spelled differently and reject the documented paths, several managed-only keys have no reader, and one documented default is deliberately inverted.

findings.claim: The sandbox write/deny path keys are nested under `sandbox.filesystem` and named `allowWrite`, `denyWrite`, `denyRead`, `allowRead`.
findings.quote: Paths in `filesystem.allowWrite`, `filesystem.denyWrite`, `filesystem.denyRead`, `filesystem.allowRead`, and `credentials.files` support these prefixes:
findings.ourState: `SANDBOX_FILESYSTEM_KEYS` is `['disabled','allowRead','allowManagedReadPathsOnly']` and the equivalents live flat at the top level under different names (`additionalWritableRoots`, `deniedWriteRoots`, `deniedReadRoots`). `filesystemSection` THROWS `invalid sandbox filesystem setting: allowWrite` on any other nested key, so a settings file written exactly as the doc shows is rejected whole at user/project/local scope.

findings.claim: Sandbox filesystem paths accept `~/`-relative and `./`-or-bare project-relative prefixes, not only absolute paths.
findings.quote: The older `//path` prefix for absolute paths still works. If you previously used single-slash `/path` expecting project-relative resolution, switch to `./path`.
findings.ourState: `filesystemRoots` rejects any non-absolute entry with `sandbox-<key>-not-absolute`, so the doc's own examples `~/.kube`, `./output` and `.` are refused.

findings.claim: `sandbox.enabled`, `sandbox.failIfUnavailable`, `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`, `sandbox.credentials`, `sandbox.bwrapPath` and `sandbox.socatPath` are settings keys.
findings.quote: | `failIfUnavailable`                    | Exit with an error at startup if `sandbox.enabled` is true but the sandbox cannot start (missing dependencies or unsupported platform).
findings.ourState: `SANDBOX_SETTING_KEYS` is `['excludedCommands','deniedReadRoots','deniedWriteRoots','additionalWritableRoots','allowUnsandboxedCommands','network','filesystem']`. None of the six exist; `managed-composition.ts` records `sandbox.bwrapPath`/`sandbox.socatPath` as having no counterpart.

findings.claim: An `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry carries an optional `autoUpdate` boolean whose omitted default is `true` for official Anthropic marketplaces and `false` for all others.
findings.quote: Each marketplace entry also accepts an optional `autoUpdate` Boolean. Set `"autoUpdate": true` alongside `source` to make Claude Code refresh that marketplace and update its installed plugins in the background after startup.
findings.ourState: `DeliveredMarketplaceEntryV1` carries only `name`, `source`, `refName`; the row parser reads `name`/`source`/`ref` and drops everything else. `skipLfs` is likewise unread, and no background marketplace/plugin auto-update exists anywhere (grep -a for `pluginAutoUpdate|updateMarketplaces|refreshMarketplace` is empty).

findings.claim: `strictKnownMarketplaces` accepts eight source types: `github`, `git`, `url`, `npm`, `file`, `directory`, `hostPattern`, `pathPattern`.
findings.quote: * `npm`, `file`, `directory`: not supported for host pattern matching
findings.ourState: `parseManagedMarketplaceEntry` handles only `github`, `url`, `hostPattern`, `pathPattern`; every other kind hits `default` and returns `managed marketplace allowlist entry declares an unsupported source`. An administrator writing the documented `{ "source": "git", "url": "https://gitlab.example.com/tools/plugins.git" }` has the entry stripped, so that marketplace can never be allowlisted in its documented form.

findings.claim: `worktree.bgIsolation` defaults to `"worktree"`.
findings.quote: `"worktree"` (default) blocks `Edit`/`Write` in the main checkout until `EnterWorktree` is called.
findings.ourState: Resolved default is `'none'` — `bgIsolation: layers.some(layer => layer.bgIsolation === 'worktree') ? 'worktree' : 'none'`. The module header records this as a deliberate fork divergence (the release valve is a Pi-only tool).

findings.claim: `policyHelper` names an executable whose stdout `managedSettings` envelope becomes the only managed source for the run, with `path`/`timeoutMs`/`refreshIntervalMs` keys and a non-zero exit refusing startup.
findings.quote: The `policyHelper` setting points at an executable that computes managed settings at startup, so admins can derive policy from device posture, identity, or a remote service instead of a static file.
findings.ourState: The identifier appears exactly once repo-wide, inside a precedence comment; there is no helper spawn, no envelope parse and no refresh timer.

findings.claim: `blockedMarketplaces` and `disableSideloadFlags` are managed-only settings enforced before download and at startup respectively.
findings.quote: (Managed settings only) Blocklist of marketplace sources. Enforced on marketplace add and on plugin install, update, refresh, and auto-update, so a marketplace added before the policy was set cannot be used to fetch plugins.
findings.ourState: Neither key exists in `MANAGED_POLICY_KEYS` nor anywhere in `packages/`/`apps/` (grep -a repo-wide hits docs only). Recorded as a known deviation in the register; the allowlist half (`strictKnownMarketplaces`) is the only managed marketplace control shipped.

findings.claim: `enableAllProjectMcpServers`, `enabledMcpjsonServers` and `disabledMcpjsonServers` gate which `.mcp.json` servers are approved.
findings.quote: Automatically approve all MCP servers defined in project `.mcp.json` files.
findings.ourState: None of the three identifiers exists outside docs. Project `.mcp.json` records are gated only by whole-workspace trust (`projectTrustState === 'trusted'`); once trusted, every declared server loads with no per-server approve/reject list.

pages.summary: Mostly a comparison of isolation approaches (dev containers, sandbox-runtime, VMs, Claude Code on the web) that we do not ship as product surfaces, but it binds two settings-level facts about the built-in sandbox that we do ship.

findings.claim: Running the sandbox inside an unprivileged container requires the nested-sandbox setting (`enableWeakerNestedSandbox`).
findings.quote: Unprivileged containers need the nested-sandbox setting described in [Sandboxing troubleshooting](/docs/en/sandboxing#troubleshooting).
findings.ourState: No such key exists in `SANDBOX_SETTING_KEYS`; `resolveLinuxIsolation` builds an `unshare`/`firejail` profile and fails closed with `process-isolation-unavailable` when the namespace cannot be created, so a supervised session cannot run inside an unprivileged container at all.

findings.claim: The built-in Bash sandbox is the only approach the product enforces itself, delivered through the `sandbox` settings keys in managed settings.
findings.quote: **Built-in Bash sandbox**: the only approach Claude Code enforces itself. Deliver the `sandbox` settings keys through [managed settings](/docs/en/settings#settings-files), either as a file managed by your MDM or through [server-managed settings](/docs/en/server-managed-settings) on Claude.ai.
findings.ourState: Managed delivery of a `sandbox` block exists and is parsed tolerantly, but the deliverable key set is a strict subset (no `enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`, `credentials`, `bwrapPath`, `socatPath`), so the documented enforcement configuration cannot be deployed verbatim.

pages.summary: The full sandbox configuration contract. Our supervised-process isolation implements the deny-read/deny-write/extra-write core, the filesystem.disabled layer switch, worktree shared-.git writes, excludedCommands and the managed read/domain locks, but the credential block, the network proxy keys and several macOS/Linux escape hatches have no reader.

findings.claim: `sandbox.credentials` declares credential files and env vars with `deny`/`mask` modes, `injectHosts`, and `allowPlaintextInject`.
findings.quote: The `sandbox.credentials` setting declares credential files and environment variables to protect from sandboxed commands.
findings.ourState: `credentials` is not in `SANDBOX_SETTING_KEYS`; the string appears only in a doc comment. `sandbox-settings.ts:321` cites the `sandbox.credentials` tolerance rule but applies it to the `network` sub-block instead. `credentials.envVars` deny/mask, `injectHosts` and `allowPlaintextInject` are all absent.

findings.claim: `network.strictAllowlist` denies sandboxed commands access to hosts outside the allowlist instead of prompting, and is honored only from user, managed or CLI settings.
findings.quote: **Strict allowlist**: {/* min-version: 2.1.219 */}if you set [`strictAllowlist`](/docs/en/settings#sandbox-settings) to `true` in user, managed, or CLI `--settings` settings, Claude Code denies sandboxed commands access to any host outside the allowlist instead of prompting.
findings.ourState: `SANDBOX_NETWORK_KEYS` is `['deniedDomains','allowedDomains','allowManagedDomainsOnly']`. `strictAllowlist` has no reader; the only fail-closed egress lever is `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, which is managed-only.

findings.claim: `network.tlsTerminate`, `network.httpProxyPort` and `network.socksProxyPort` configure the sandbox egress proxy.
findings.quote: To point Claude Code at your proxy, set the proxy ports in [sandbox settings](/docs/en/settings#sandbox-settings):
findings.ourState: None of the three keys is in `SANDBOX_NETWORK_KEYS`; a settings file containing them is rejected at strict scope and stripped at managed scope. There is no sandbox egress proxy — `resolveSandboxNetworkEnforcement` returns `'open' | 'denied'` only.

findings.claim: `allowAppleEvents`, `enableWeakerNetworkIsolation`, `enableWeakerNestedSandbox`, `network.allowUnixSockets`, `network.allowAllUnixSockets`, `network.allowLocalBinding` and `network.allowMachLookup` are sandbox settings.
findings.quote: Set [`allowAppleEvents`](/docs/en/settings#sandbox-settings) to `true` in your user, managed, or CLI settings to allow them.
findings.ourState: None of the seven identifiers exists in `packages/` or `apps/` source (the only `allowUnixSockets`/`allowLocalBinding` hits are in `packages/codex-protocol/generated/v2/NetworkRequirements.ts`, an unrelated Codex wire type). The documented workarounds for `open`/`osascript` error -600, Go-tool TLS failures and unprivileged containers are unavailable.

findings.claim: `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` defaults to `true` and can be set to `false` to keep prompting for sandboxed commands.
findings.quote: [`autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`](/docs/en/settings#sandbox-settings) still defaults to `true`, so sandboxed commands keep running without prompts. Set it to `false` to keep prompting for sandboxed commands.
findings.ourState: No such key. Recorded as a deliberate refusal in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-29-deviation-unit-5.md:115`: the documented default is conditioned on `sandbox.enabled`, which this fork has no analogue of, so shipping the key verbatim would auto-approve every Bash command.

findings.claim: The sandbox settings-file write denies resolve symlinks, so a symlink appearing at a protected settings path has its target added to the deny list for the next command.
findings.quote: The deny rules resolve symlinks: when a symlink appears at a protected settings file path after startup, the sandbox adds its target to the deny list for the next command, so a linked settings file can't be edited through the link.
findings.ourState: `selfConfigDenyWriteRoots` builds the deny set lexically; the file contains no `realpath`, `lstat` or symlink handling, so a settings file symlinked out of the protected directory stays writable from inside the sandbox.

pages.summary: The SDK-side MCP contract. Our pool implements transports, backoff, list_changed, idle timeout and per-server timeout, but the `streamable-http` type alias is missing from our own reader and the output-token limit differs from the documented default with no env override.

findings.claim: `"streamable-http"` is accepted as an alias for `"http"` in `.mcp.json` and other JSON config files.
findings.quote: In `.mcp.json` and other JSON config files, `"streamable-http"` is accepted as an alias for `"http"`.
findings.ourState: `parseProjectMcpServer` branches on `type === 'http' || type === 'sse'`, then `'ws'`, then `undefined|'stdio'`, and returns `null` for anything else — the caller logs `Ignoring .mcp.json server "<name>": unsupported MCP server config` and drops it. The Claude plugin adapter has the same closed set. The alias exists only inside the vendored Pi/session-MCP bundles under `apps/electron/dist`, never in our own parser.

findings.claim: MCP tool results larger than 25,000 tokens are persisted to disk, and the limit is raised with `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`.
findings.quote: When a tool result is larger than 25,000 tokens, the full output is saved to a file and the tool result is replaced with an error message that names the file path, so the agent can read the output back in portions.
findings.ourState: `TOKEN_LIMIT = 12000` is the persist threshold and there is no `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` (or Nessy-prefixed) env reader anywhere. The per-tool `_meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"]` half IS implemented, clamped to the documented 500,000 ceiling.

findings.claim: `MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=0` restores a bounded startup wait capped at 5 seconds by `MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`.
findings.quote: To restore a bounded startup wait for every server, set the [`MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING`](/docs/en/env-vars) environment variable to `0`. The wait is capped at 5 seconds by [`MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS`](/docs/en/env-vars), and servers still pending at that deadline keep connecting in the background.
findings.ourState: `MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING` has no reader. `MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS` exists only as a module constant of 30_000 ms (the per-server connect deadline), not as an env var and not as a 5-second startup cap — same identifier, different meaning and default.

pages.summary: The allowlist/denylist half of the contract — entry shapes, URL wildcards, ${VAR} expansion, the per-type allowlist table and `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` — is implemented faithfully in `managed-mcp-entries.ts`. The `managed-mcp.json` deployment channel and its exclusive-control mode are not.

findings.claim: A `managed-mcp.json` file at a system path takes exclusive control: only its servers load, and `claude mcp add` is refused.
findings.quote: If you deploy a `managed-mcp.json` file, Claude Code loads only the servers that file defines. Users cannot add, modify, or use any other MCP servers, including plugin-provided servers.
findings.ourState: No reader for the file at any of the three documented system paths (grep -a for `managed-mcp.json` hits docs and comments only). There is no exclusive-control mode and therefore no way to express the documented "disable MCP entirely" pattern — `deniedMcpServers` blocks only what it names. Recorded in docs/architecture/managed-mcp-access.md:91.

findings.claim: A denylist match blocks a server by URL, command, or name, and nothing overrides it.
findings.quote: **Check the denylist.** A server that matches any denylist entry, by URL, command, or name, is blocked. Nothing overrides a denylist match.
findings.ourState: `isManagedMcpServerAllowed` enforces all three key forms correctly, but the channel-push gate `resolveManagedChannelPolicy` folds in only the `serverName` entries of `deniedMcpServers`, because it is keyed on a source slug. A `serverUrl`/`serverCommand` deny does not reach that gate; the module comment states this enforces strictly less than the policy.

findings.claim: `allowAllClaudeAiMcps` loads claude.ai connectors alongside the managed set and is read only from admin-controlled policy tiers.
findings.quote: To load those connectors alongside the servers in `managed-mcp.json`, set `"allowAllClaudeAiMcps": true` in a [managed settings source](/docs/en/admin-setup#decide-how-settings-reach-devices).
findings.ourState: No counterpart in `ManagedPiPolicyV1`; recorded as inapplicable because this fork has no claude.ai account-side connectors (a deliberate product difference), and `managed-composition.ts` already names it as having nothing to compose.

pages.summary: The full MCP reference. Transports, scopes, ${VAR} expansion, OAuth overrides, per-server timeout, idle timeout, auto-backgrounding, alwaysLoad, elicitation, list_changed and the _meta annotations are implemented. Missing: the `streamable-http` alias, `roots/list`, `headersHelper`, reserved server names, and the project `.mcp.json` per-server approval lists.

findings.claim: Claude Code answers `roots/list` with the launch directory plus every additional working directory, and sends `notifications/roots/list_changed` when that set changes.
findings.quote: Claude Code answers `roots/list` with the session's launch directory plus every [additional working directory](/docs/en/permissions#working-directories) you've granted with `--add-dir`, `/add-dir`, or the `additionalDirectories` setting.
findings.ourState: The MCP client is constructed with `capabilities: options?.elicitationHandler ? { elicitation: { form: {}, url: {} } } : {}` — the `roots` capability is never advertised, so `roots/list` is never requested and no `list_changed` roots notification is emitted. A server that scopes its own filesystem access via roots gets nothing. Confirmed absent repo-wide with `grep -a`.

findings.claim: `"streamable-http"` is a valid value of the `type` field wherever MCP servers are configured in JSON.
findings.quote: When configuring MCP servers via JSON in `.mcp.json`, `~/.claude.json`, or `claude mcp add-json`, the `type` field accepts `streamable-http` as an alias for `http`.
findings.ourState: Our `.mcp.json` parser and the Claude plugin adapter both accept only `stdio|http|sse|ws`; an entry copied verbatim from an MCP server's own documentation is dropped with `unsupported MCP server config`.

findings.claim: `headersHelper` runs a command at connection time whose stdout JSON is merged into the connection headers, with `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME`/`CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL`/`CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` in its environment and a 10-second timeout.
findings.quote: If your MCP server uses an authentication scheme other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO, use `headersHelper` to generate request headers at connection time.
findings.ourState: Not implemented for any transport. Both readers detect the field and emit a warning (`"headersHelper" is not implemented for any transport; it was ignored`) and a deferred-capability record; the server still connects with static headers only.

findings.claim: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` servers require per-server approval before use, resettable with `claude mcp reset-project-choices`.
findings.quote: For security reasons, Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from `.mcp.json` files.
findings.ourState: The only gate is whole-workspace trust; inside a trusted project every `.mcp.json` server is materialized without an individual approve/reject step, and none of `enabledMcpjsonServers`, `disabledMcpjsonServers`, `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or a reset command exists.

findings.claim: A fixed set of server names is reserved and a configuration defining one is skipped with a warning.
findings.quote: Some server names are reserved for Claude Code's built-in servers: `workspace`, `claude-in-chrome`, `computer-use`, `Claude Preview`, and `Claude Browser`.
findings.ourState: No reserved-name check anywhere in the `.mcp.json` reader or the plugin adapter; a plugin or project file may register any name, including one colliding with a bundled session server.

pages.summary: An onboarding walkthrough of the `claude mcp` CLI, which this fork does not ship (our CLI has validate/list/details only). The parts that bind a surface we do ship are the `.mcp.json` document shape, the 30-second startup timeout and the project-server approval prompt.

findings.claim: The MCP server startup timeout is 30 seconds by default and is raised with the `MCP_TIMEOUT` environment variable in milliseconds.
findings.quote: The server took longer than the default 30-second startup timeout. A stdio server's first run can be slow while `npx` downloads the package. Increase the limit with the [`MCP_TIMEOUT`](/docs/en/env-vars) environment variable, in milliseconds:
findings.ourState: The 30 s default matches (`MCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`), but it is a compile-time constant overridable only through a programmatic `connectTimeoutMs` option — there is no `MCP_TIMEOUT` (or Nessy-prefixed) env reader, so an operator cannot raise it.

findings.claim: A project-scoped server awaiting approval is reported as pending, and a rejected one is attributed to `disabledMcpjsonServers`.
findings.quote: `claude mcp get <name>` shows rejected servers as `✘ Rejected (see disabledMcpjsonServers in settings)`.
findings.ourState: No pending/rejected state exists for project MCP servers; workspace trust is the whole gate and `disabledMcpjsonServers` has no reader. Same root cause as the mcp.md finding.

pages.summary: Binds the SDK `plugins` option (`type: "local"` + path), the optional manifest, and skill namespacing. We deliberately pass an empty `plugins` array to the Claude SDK and project plugin capabilities through our own runtime instead; the manifest-optional rule is honored by our adapter.

findings.claim: Plugins are loaded into a session by passing local paths in the `plugins` option, and their skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers become available to that session.
findings.quote: Load plugins by providing their local file system paths in your options configuration. The `type` field must be `"local"`, the only value the SDK accepts.
findings.ourState: `plugins: []` is hardcoded on every Claude SDK query, with the comment "No plugins — skills are handled by BaseAgent.chat() via read-before-execute". Plugin skills/MCP/hooks reach a Claude-backed session only through the capability runtime and the automation hook bridge, never through the SDK's own plugin loader. This is a deliberate architectural substitution, not an oversight, but it means SDK-side plugin behaviors (init-message `plugins` list, `/plugin-name:skill-name` dispatch) do not exist on that path.

pages.summary: Install scopes, marketplace add sources and the managed marketplace keys are implemented. The auto-update subsystem, its two env-var switches, and the contextual-suggestion allowlist have no reader.

findings.claim: Marketplaces and their installed plugins auto-update in the background after startup, on by default for official Anthropic marketplaces and off by default for third-party and local ones.
findings.quote: Official Anthropic marketplaces have auto-update enabled by default. Third-party and local development marketplaces have auto-update disabled by default.
findings.ourState: No background marketplace or plugin update path exists — `grep -a` for `pluginAutoUpdate|autoUpdatePlugins|backgroundPluginUpdate|updateMarketplaces|refreshMarketplace` across `packages/` and `apps/` returns nothing, and the only `autoUpdate` hits are the Electron app updater. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` and `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS` are likewise unread. Consequently the per-entry default the doc specifies is unobservable.
findings.evidence: packages/shared/src/plugins/store-v2.ts:154 (update journal exists; nothing schedules against it)

findings.claim: `pluginSuggestionMarketplaces` is a managed allowlist gating whether a plugin's marketplace-entry `relevance` block can surface as a contextual install suggestion.
findings.quote: When your administrator has allowlisted the marketplace via the [`pluginSuggestionMarketplaces`](/docs/en/settings#available-settings) managed setting, plugins marked as relevant to your current working directory are pinned at the top with a **suggested for this directory** label.
findings.ourState: Neither the setting nor a contextual-suggestion surface exists; the `relevance` field is dropped at catalog parse. Recorded as a deliberate deferral in the deviation register (line 183).

findings.claim: Removing a marketplace uninstalls the plugins installed from it.
findings.quote: Removing a marketplace will uninstall any plugins you installed from it.
findings.ourState: Registry removal drops the source and its catalog; installed-record cleanup runs through `store.prune()` on inactive instances rather than an explicit uninstall of the marketplace's plugins, so the cascade is not the documented one. Worth a targeted test rather than a code change.

pages.summary: The load-time half — declared dependencies, semver ranges, the three error codes, enable-with-dependencies and disable-refusal — is implemented and cites this page line by line. The resolution half (auto-install, git-tag version resolution, cross-marketplace allowlist, prune) is deliberately deferred with the reason recorded in code.

findings.claim: Installing a plugin that declares dependencies resolves and installs them automatically, fetching each at the highest `{plugin-name}--v{version}` git tag that satisfies the range.
findings.quote: When you install a plugin that declares dependencies, Claude Code resolves and installs them automatically and lists which dependencies were added at the end of the install output.
findings.ourState: No auto-install and no tag enumeration. The module header records the reason: no marketplace source in this repo enumerates git tags, so resolving a range against "whatever the catalog currently holds" would make `~2.1.0` silently mean latest. A declared dependency that is not already installed surfaces as `dependency-unsatisfied` and disables the dependent plugin.

findings.claim: A cross-marketplace dependency is refused unless the root marketplace lists the target in `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn`.
findings.quote: To allow it, the maintainer of the root marketplace adds the target marketplace name to `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn` in `marketplace.json`.
findings.ourState: The field is not carried past catalog parse and no `cross-marketplace` error exists; the adapter comment records that with nothing auto-installed there is no install to refuse, and the `marketplace` field on each dependency is carried so the check has its input the day auto-install lands.

findings.claim: When several installed plugins constrain the same dependency, the ranges are intersected and an unsatisfiable combination fails the install with `range-conflict`.
findings.quote: When several installed plugins constrain the same dependency, Claude Code intersects their ranges and resolves the dependency to the highest version that satisfies all of them.
findings.ourState: No intersection. Each dependent's range is checked independently against the installed version, which produces the same per-plugin verdict without a fetch. `range-conflict` is emitted only for the other documented cause — an unparseable semver range.

findings.claim: `claude plugin tag`, `claude plugin prune` and `claude plugin uninstall --prune` manage release tags and orphaned auto-installed dependencies.
findings.quote: Auto-installed dependencies stay on disk after the plugins that installed them are uninstalled, in case you reinstall a dependent plugin or want to keep using the dependency directly.
findings.ourState: The CLI exposes only `validate`, `list`/`ls`, `details` and `help`; there is no `tag`, `prune`, `install`, `uninstall`, `enable` or `disable` subcommand. `store.prune()` is cache GC of inactive plugin instances, not orphan-dependency removal — and with no auto-install there are no orphans to remove.

pages.summary: Describes the `<claude-code-hint />` stderr marker protocol by which a third-party CLI asks the agent to prompt a plugin install. Nessy has no reader for the marker and does not set the environment variable that would make a CLI emit it, so the surface is absent end to end; the marketplace half is Anthropic-curated and deliberately out of scope for this fork.

findings.claim: The agent must scan Bash/PowerShell tool output for a self-closing `<claude-code-hint v="1" type="plugin" value="name@marketplace" />` line, strip it before the output reaches the model, and (optionally) act on it.
findings.quote: The hint line is always removed from the output before it reaches the model, even when the version or type is unrecognized, so the marker is never counted toward token usage.
findings.ourState: No code path recognises or strips the marker. `grep -ran "claude-code-hint" .` over the whole repo returns exactly one hit, in a docs note (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-26-r-queue-doc-verification.md`), and zero hits under `packages/` or `apps/`. Practically inert today because we also never set the gating env var (see next finding), but any CLI that gates on a variable we do inherit would leak the raw tag into model context.

findings.claim: Every subprocess the Bash/PowerShell tool and hook commands spawn carries an environment marker announcing that it is running inside the coding agent; third-party CLIs gate behaviour on it.
findings.quote: Claude Code sets the [`CLAUDECODE`](/docs/en/env-vars) environment variable to `1` for every command it runs through the Bash and PowerShell tools, and for [hook](/docs/en/hooks) commands.
findings.ourState: Nessy sets no equivalent marker in tool subprocesses. The only `CLAUDECODE` references in the repo REMOVE it from a child env (`apps/cli/src/server-spawner.ts:62` strips it to dodge the Claude SDK nesting guard) and there is no `NESSYCODE`/`NESSY_CODE` replacement anywhere. This is not the ordinary brand-prefix rename: the variable is read by third-party tools, not by us, so no NESSY_-prefixed name substitutes for it, and CLIs that adapt their output for agent use (non-interactive mode, no colour, machine-readable output) do not adapt for Nessy.

pages.summary: Marketplace catalog schema, plugin source types, strict mode, version resolution, `renames`, and managed restrictions. The core is matched closely (all five source types, `sha`-over-`ref` pinning, `metadata.pluginRoot`, `renames` chains, `strict`, `plugin.json`-wins version order, `strictKnownMarketplaces`/`extraKnownMarketplaces`); the entry-field carry list drops six documented fields, and three operator-facing subsystems are absent.

findings.claim: A marketplace plugin entry may carry `category`, `tags`, `relevance` (marketplace-specific) plus any manifest field including `license`, `keywords`, `repository`.
findings.quote: You can include any field from the [plugin manifest schema](/docs/en/plugins-reference#plugin-manifest-schema), such as `description`, `version`, `author`, `commands`, and `hooks`, plus these marketplace-specific fields: `source`, `category`, `tags`, `strict`, and `relevance`.
findings.ourState: `MARKETPLACE_ENTRY_CARRIED_FIELDS` carries only the path fields plus `displayName`, `description`, `version`, `author`, `homepage`, `defaultEnabled`, `dependencies`. `category`, `tags`, `relevance`, `license`, `keywords` and `repository` are dropped at catalog parse and never reach the adapter — grep for `'category'`/`'tags'`/`'license'`/`'keywords'` in that file returns zero. `category` and `tags` are the documented organisation/search axes, so a marketplace that categorises its plugins loses that in our Discover list.

findings.claim: A marketplace may declare which other marketplaces its plugins are allowed to depend on, and a dependency outside that list is refused at install.
findings.quote: Dependencies from a marketplace not listed here are blocked at install.
findings.ourState: `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn` has no reader anywhere in `packages/` or `apps/` — the only hits are in two plan documents and one comment (`format-adapters/claude.ts:1577`) that names it as unbuilt. Recorded as a deliberate deferral in the deviation register: with no dependency auto-install there is no install edge for the allowlist to gate.

findings.claim: A pre-populated, read-only plugins directory can be pointed at with an environment variable so container/CI images start with marketplaces and plugin caches already present, with a second variable to install directly into that path at build time.
findings.quote: Set the `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR` environment variable to point at this directory.
findings.ourState: No seed-directory concept exists. `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR`, `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR`, `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_GIT_TIMEOUT_MS` and `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_PREFER_HTTPS` all return zero hits under `--include='*.ts'` repo-wide, and there is no NESSY_-prefixed equivalent for any of them. The offline/airgap escape hatch the page recommends (`KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE`) therefore has no counterpart, which matters for a corporate-network fork.

findings.claim: A fixed list of marketplace names is reserved and re-checked on every load, so a third-party catalog cannot register under a name that impersonates an official one.
findings.quote: Claude Code re-checks reserved names every time it loads a marketplace, not only when you add one.
findings.ourState: No reserved-name list and no name-impersonation check exists: grep for `RESERVED_MARKETPLACE`/`reserved` under `packages/shared/src/marketplace/` and `packages/shared/src/plugins/` returns nothing. Partly a brand artefact (the reserved names are Anthropic's), but the mechanism — a name-collision guard on registration — has no Nessy analogue either, so an imported catalog can register under any name including our own delivered-marketplace names.

pages.summary: Specifies the `relevance` block on a marketplace plugin entry (topic plus `cwd`/`cli`/`hosts`/`filesRead`/`manifestDeps` signals), the local signal matching, the three surfaces it feeds, and the managed-settings allowlist that gates it. Nessy drops the field at catalog parse and has none of the surfaces; this is a recorded owner decision, not an oversight.

findings.claim: A marketplace entry may carry a `relevance` object with a `topic` and one or more of five signal matchers, matched locally against session state.
findings.quote: Each plugin entry in `marketplace.json` can carry a `relevance` object.
findings.ourState: `relevance` is dropped at catalog parse — it is absent from `MARKETPLACE_ENTRY_CARRIED_FIELDS` and the only occurrence of the word in `packages/` is a doc comment in `plugins/types.ts:832` quoting the marketplace page. None of `cwd`/`cli`/`hosts`/`filesRead`/`manifestDeps` matching exists. Recorded deliberately in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-register.md:183` ("Nessy has no contextual plugin-suggestion surface for the signals to feed, so the field is dropped at catalog parse rather than carried into a definition nothing reads").

findings.claim: An administrator allowlists marketplaces for suggestions via a managed setting, and a name is honoured only when the marketplace registered on the machine came from the declared source.
findings.quote: Add the marketplace name to `pluginSuggestionMarketplaces`.
findings.ourState: `pluginSuggestionMarketplaces` has no reader: a repo-wide `grep -ran` (excluding node_modules and .git) hits only two plan/spec documents. The sibling managed keys it composes with — `extraKnownMarketplaces`, `strictKnownMarketplaces`, `blockedMarketplaces` — ARE implemented (`packages/shared/src/marketplace/registry-source.ts:163-175`), so the gap is specific to the suggestion allowlist rather than to managed marketplace policy generally.

pages.summary: The authoring tutorial for plugins, plus three binding sections: the plugin-root directory table (including `bin/` and `settings.json`), local testing flags, and community-marketplace submission. Component discovery matches; two plugin-root surfaces named in the directory table are recorded-but-not-loaded, and the local-testing flags have no desktop equivalent.

findings.claim: A plugin may ship a `settings.json` at its root whose `agent` key activates one of the plugin's own subagents as the main thread, and whose values outrank a `settings` block in `plugin.json`.
findings.quote: Plugins can include a `settings.json` file at the plugin root to apply default configuration when the plugin is enabled. Currently, only the `agent` and `subagentStatusLine` keys are supported.
findings.ourState: The file is detected and recorded as a deferral only — `CLAUDE_RETAINED_SURFACE_FIELDS` carries `{ externalKind: 'settings', field: 'settings', defaultPath: 'settings.json' }`, which pushes a `plugin.deferred.claude_settings` row and nothing else. Neither key is read anywhere: `grep -ran "subagentStatusLine" --include='*.ts' .` returns zero hits repo-wide. A plugin whose whole purpose is to change the main thread's agent installs and silently does nothing.

findings.claim: Executables in a plugin's `bin/` are added to the Bash tool's PATH and invokable as bare commands while the plugin is enabled.
findings.quote: Executables added to the Bash tool's `PATH`. Files here are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call while the plugin is enabled
findings.ourState: Recorded as a deferral and deliberately not implemented — `{ externalKind: 'bin', defaultPath: 'bin' }` with the in-file reason "Nessy never extends PATH from a bundle". This is a dated owner recommendation (parity audit row B1): a plugin dropping a file named `git`/`ssh`/`sudo` into `bin/` would shadow it for every subprocess we spawn, and the plugin need only be enabled, never invoked. Listed here because the doc binds it, not because it should change.

findings.claim: A plugin can be loaded for one session from a local directory or a `.zip`, and from a remote `.zip` URL, with the local copy outranking a same-named installed plugin.
findings.quote: The flag also accepts a `.zip` archive of the plugin directory, which requires Claude Code v2.1.128 or later.
findings.ourState: No session-scoped sideload path exists. `--plugin-dir`/`--plugin-url` and any equivalent have no reader: the only `pluginDir` symbols in the repo are internal catalog paths (`packages/shared/src/plugins/registry-catalog-fetcher.ts:385`, `packages/shared/src/workspaces/storage.ts:284`), not a load-for-this-session flag. Partly a shape difference (we are a desktop app, not a CLI), but the developer loop the page prescribes — edit, relaunch pointed at the directory, no install — has no counterpart, and `disableSideloadFlags` (the managed key that would refuse it) is correspondingly absent too.

pages.summary: The full component/manifest/CLI contract. Our Claude adapter matches this page unusually closely — every manifest field, the REPLACES/ADDS path rules, the 30-event hook table (28 emitted, 2 recorded deferrals), monitor `when`, `userConfig` types, `defaultEnabled` precedence, `displayName`, version resolution order and the `lspServers` field name are all present and cited in-file. Four surfaces remain unbuilt, three of them with recorded reasons.

findings.claim: A folder under a skills directory containing `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` loads as a plugin named `<name>@skills-dir` with no marketplace and no install step, discovered in place rather than copied into the cache.
findings.quote: Any folder under a skills directory that contains a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest is loaded as a plugin named `<name>@skills-dir` on the next session, with no marketplace and no install step.
findings.ourState: Not implemented. `grep -ran "skills-dir"` over the repo hits only plan/spec prose — including `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-audit.md:197` which itself records "skills-dir plugins undetected (B1, still not started)". Skill discovery walks `.claude/skills` at project and ancestor depth (`native-sources.ts` line ~1065, tagged `d${depth}`) but never checks a skill folder for a plugin manifest, so a bundle laid out this way contributes its SKILL.md and silently drops its agents, hooks and MCP servers.

findings.claim: Eight optional LSP fields govern server lifecycle and diagnostics injection, two of them with defaults (`restartOnCrash` defaults to `true`, `diagnostics` defaults to `true`).
findings.quote: `restartOnCrash`        | Whether to restart the server after it crashes. Defaults to `true`. Set to `false` to leave a crashed server stopped instead of restarting it
findings.ourState: All eight are parsed as declared-but-unread: `CLAUDE_UNREAD_LSP_FIELDS` lists `transport`, `initializationOptions`, `settings`, `startupTimeout`, `shutdownTimeout`, `restartOnCrash`, `maxRestarts`, `diagnostics`, and the reader emits a `plugin.format.claude_lsp_fields_unread` warning naming them. The capability that reaches the runtime carries only `command`, `args`, `languages`, `env`, `workspaceFolder`. An author who sets `diagnostics: false` to suppress automatic diagnostic injection, or `restartOnCrash: false` on a server that crash-loops, gets neither.

findings.claim: `userConfig` values are substituted as `${user_config.KEY}` into MCP and LSP server configs and (for non-sensitive values) into skill and agent content.
findings.quote: Each value is available for substitution as `${user_config.KEY}` in MCP and LSP server configs and hook commands.
findings.ourState: The option schema, the sensitivity split, the storage-source restriction and the `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` export are all built; the `${user_config.*}` substitution into MCP/LSP configs and skill/agent content is not, and the surface carries its own deferral row `plugin.deferred.claude_user_config_substitution`. A plugin whose MCP server config references `${user_config.api_endpoint}` therefore starts with the literal placeholder.

findings.claim: A plugin may ship colour themes in `themes/` that appear in `/theme`, selected as `custom:<plugin-name>:<slug>`.
findings.quote: Plugins can ship color themes that appear in `/theme` alongside the built-in presets and the user's local themes.
findings.ourState: Deliberately REFUSED rather than loaded, with an author-facing `plugin.format.claude_theme_unsupported` warning at install. The recorded reason (in-file, 20 lines) is that the documented theme is a terminal palette with a `base` preset and tokens keyed `claude`/`error`/`success`, while Nessy's theming is a web token set where `base` has no counterpart, so any mapping would be invented. Listed because the page binds it; the refusal is the decision, not a defect.

findings.claim: The `channels` field lets a plugin declare message channels bound to one of its own MCP servers, each with optional per-channel `userConfig`.
findings.quote: The `channels` field lets a plugin declare one or more message channels that inject content into the conversation.
findings.ourState: Recorded as a bare deferral (`{ externalKind: 'channel', field: 'channels' }`) with no reader for the `server` binding or the per-channel `userConfig`. There is no channel injection surface in Nessy for it to feed.

pages.summary: Specifies how the Agent SDK discovers and filters skills: filesystem-only, governed by `settingSources`, filtered by the `skills` option, with `allowed-tools` frontmatter explicitly NOT applied through the SDK. Our Claude backend takes the documented defaults, which is correct per the page but means SDK-discovered skills bypass Nessy's own capability gating.

findings.claim: Omitting the `skills` option enables every discovered user and project skill from the filesystem locations `settingSources` names; passing a list or `[]` is the only way to narrow it.
findings.quote: When omitted, discovered Skills are enabled and the Skill tool is available, matching CLI behavior.
findings.ourState: `buildClaudeSessionOptions` returns only `systemPrompt`, `settingSources` and (for a child) `maxTurns`; `skills` is never set, and `settingSources` is spelled `['user', 'project', 'local']`. So every `SKILL.md` under `~/.claude/skills/` and `<cwd>/.claude/skills/` is enabled inside a Claude-backend session, chosen by the SDK rather than by Nessy's capability resolver — the resolver's own visibility state, `enabled:false` policy and skill listing do not reach that set. Conformant with this page; the divergence is that Nessy has a second, authoritative skill-gating system that the Claude backend does not project onto the SDK.

pages.summary: The skills contract: locations and precedence, the 17-field frontmatter table, string substitutions, dynamic context injection, forked execution, and the settings that govern visibility and listing budget. Frontmatter parsing is near-exact (including the v2.1.218 loose booleans and the 1,536-char cap constant); four frontmatter fields are parsed-and-ignored by design, three settings keys have no reader at all, and the dynamic-context syntax we accept is not the documented one.

findings.claim: Dynamic context uses an inline `` !`<command>` `` placeholder that may appear anywhere in the body, whose output replaces the placeholder in place, with a ` ```! ` fenced block for multi-line commands.
findings.quote: The `` !`<command>` `` syntax runs shell commands before the skill content is sent to Claude.
findings.ourState: `runtimeSkillContextCommand` recognises a different syntax: a bare `!command` that must be the FIRST non-empty top-level body line, backticks not part of the form, fenced blocks skipped as prose, and a second `!` line throwing `runtime-skill-context-command-ambiguous`. Output is appended (`outputs.join('\n\n')`) rather than substituted at the placeholder. The docs' own example skill (`- PR diff: !`gh pr diff``, three placeholders inside list items) yields zero substitutions here; a skill whose first line IS `` !`git diff HEAD` `` passes the backticks through to the Bash permission evaluator as part of the command string.

findings.claim: Dynamic context injection applies to skills and custom commands from user, project, plugin and additional-directory sources.
findings.quote: To disable this behavior for skills and custom commands from user, project, plugin, or [additional-directory](#skills-from-additional-directories) sources, set `"disableSkillShellExecution": true` in [settings](/docs/en/settings).
findings.ourState: Two divergences on one line. (1) Our executor runs only for skills with `skill.pluginRuntime` set and only when `runtime?.provider === 'pi'` — a user or project skill, and any skill on the Claude backend, never executes its command. (2) `disableSkillShellExecution` has no reader anywhere in the repo, so the managed-settings kill switch the page recommends for exactly this capability cannot be applied.

findings.claim: A settings key overrides per-skill visibility from settings rather than frontmatter, with four states, absent meaning `on`, and `off` also hiding the skill from SDK and Remote-Control command lists.
findings.quote: The `skillOverrides` setting controls skill visibility from your [settings](/docs/en/settings) instead of the skill's own frontmatter.
findings.ourState: No reader. `grep -ran "skillOverrides"` over the repo hits only two planning documents (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-29-session-scheduling.md:193` and the r-queue verification spec). None of the four states exists, so the only way to hide a skill checked into a shared repo is to edit its SKILL.md.

findings.claim: The skill listing has a character budget that scales with the model's context window, is raisable by a settings key or an environment variable, and caps each entry's combined `description` + `when_to_use` at 1,536 characters.
findings.quote: To raise the budget, set the [`skillListingBudgetFraction`](/docs/en/settings#available-settings) setting (e.g. `0.02` = 2%) or the `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET` environment variable to a fixed character count.
findings.ourState: None of `skillListingBudgetFraction`, `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET` or `skillListingMaxDescChars` has a reader. The 1,536 constant exists (`MAX_DERIVED_DESCRIPTION_CHARS`) but is applied only as a ceiling on a description DERIVED from the body, not to the listing entry; the listing path instead clamps each catalog entry's description at a hard 512 chars (`capability-catalog.ts:107`, `clampedText(input.description, 'description', 512, …)`) with no context-window scaling and no per-entry cap of 1,536.

findings.claim: Four frontmatter fields govern where and how a skill runs: `context: fork`, `background` (default `true` for a fork as of v2.1.218), `hooks` scoped to the skill's lifecycle, and `shell: bash|powershell` for inline command blocks.
findings.quote: Add `context: fork` to your frontmatter when you want a skill to run in isolation.
findings.ourState: All four are explicitly parsed-and-dropped: `IGNORED_SKILL_FIELDS` maps `context` → 'skills do not run in a forked subagent context here', `background` → "it only applies with 'context: fork', which is not implemented", `hooks` → 'per-skill hook scopes are not implemented', `shell` → 'inline shell blocks always run under bash'. The list is deliberate and documented in-file; a skill that sets `context: fork` runs inline in the main conversation instead of in an isolated subagent, which is a behaviour inversion rather than a no-op.

findings.claim: A skill in a nested `.claude/skills/` below the working directory loads lazily under a directory-qualified name when Claude touches a file in that subtree, and both variants stay available when names clash.
findings.quote: The nested one appears under a directory-qualified name, `apps/web:deploy`.
findings.ourState: Not implemented. Skill discovery walks `.claude/skills` at the working directory and its ANCESTORS (`skillRecords(join(dir, PROJECT_AGENT_SKILLS_DIR), projectScope, \`d${depth}\`, …)`), which satisfies the parent-directory half, but there is no descendant scan, no lazy load on file touch, and no directory-qualified naming — `grep -ran "directory-qualified\|qualified name"` under `packages/` returns nothing relevant. A monorepo package's own skills are unreachable unless the session starts in that package.

findings.claim: Several user-invocable skills can be stacked at the start of one message; the first plus up to five more expand and each receives the trailing text as `$ARGUMENTS`.
findings.quote: Typing `/write-tests /fix-issue 123` loads both skills and passes the trailing text `123` as `$ARGUMENTS` to each of them.
findings.ourState: No stacked-invocation expansion exists: grep for `stacked`/`stack.*skill` across `packages/shared/src/capabilities`, `packages/shared/src/skills` and `packages/server-core/src` returns one unrelated comment. Argument substitution itself is complete (`$ARGUMENTS`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]`, `$N`, named `arguments`, `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`, `${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}`, `${CLAUDE_EFFORT}`, `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` are all in `runtime-skill-content.ts`), so the gap is the multi-skill prefix parse only.

pages.summary: Message lifecycle, turn definition, tool execution and parallelism, the turn/budget/effort/permission-mode/model knobs, context accumulation and compaction, and result subtypes. Every contract claim I checked is satisfied: the five effort levels including `xhigh` and `max` (`thinking-levels.ts:33-34`, `THINKING_TO_EFFORT`), the budget cap applied in the shared base agent so it covers all backends (`base-agent.ts:373-406, 2798-2832`, terminal reason `max_budget_usd`), `error_max_structured_output_retries` (`packages/core/src/types/message.ts:988`), `stop_reason` resolved before subtype so a `success` result carrying `refusal` is not reported as clean (`event-adapter.ts` result branch), `readOnlyHint` annotations carried through the MCP descriptor cache, and the `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` tool names matching the current spelling.

Specifies what `settingSources` loads per source and — the load-bearing half — the four inputs read REGARDLESS of it: managed policy, `~/.claude.json`, auto memory, and claude.ai MCP connectors, each with a named suppression knob. Our Claude backend opts into all three sources explicitly and sets none of the four suppressors.

findings.claim: Auto memory under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` and claude.ai MCP connectors load regardless of `settingSources`, and each has a named opt-out that the host must set.
findings.quote: Because the inputs above are read regardless of `settingSources`, an SDK process can pick up host-level configuration and per-directory memory.
findings.ourState: `buildClaudeSessionOptions` sets `settingSources: ['user', 'project', 'local']` and nothing else. None of `autoMemoryEnabled`, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY`, `disableClaudeAiConnectors`, `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS` or `strictMcpConfig` appears anywhere in the repo (repo-wide `grep -ran` excluding node_modules returns zero). Consequences for this fork specifically: a Claude-backend session writes memories into `~/.claude/projects/`, outside Nessy's config dir and outside its capability inventory; and when the opt-in Claude Pro/Max login is used, the user's claude.ai MCP connectors attach to the session without passing Nessy's MCP source approval, which `mcpServers: {}` explicitly does not suppress.

findings.claim: With `settingSources` including `"project"`, hooks from the workspace's own `.claude/settings.json` execute inside the SDK session with no extra configuration.
findings.quote: If you already have hooks in your project's `.claude/settings.json` and you set `settingSources: ["project"]`, those hooks run automatically in the SDK with no extra configuration.
findings.ourState: We opt into `'project'` and `'local'` unconditionally, so a cloned repository's `.claude/settings.json` hooks run in a Claude-backend session. Nessy has its own project-trust gate for exactly this class of content — `native-sources.ts:995` reads project resources only when `context.projectTrustState === 'trusted'` — but that gate governs the Nessy capability runtime, not the Claude SDK subprocess, which reads the same files independently. The two trust boundaries disagree for the same directory.

pages.summary: Defines the scoping of usage data, the three result-level fields' differing treatment of subagent spend, per-step deduplication by message ID, cache-token fields, and the 1-hour cache TTL variable. Our Claude event adapter matches the important parts — it dedupes implicitly by overwriting `lastAssistantUsage` per assistant message, carries the whole `modelUsage` map with the doc's own reasoning cited in-file, reads both cache-token fields, and takes cost from `total_cost_usd` on every result subtype.

findings.claim: The result-level `usage` field excludes subagent tokens, so a surfaced total built from it undercounts as soon as the session nests.
findings.quote: Use `modelUsage`, or `model_usage` in Python, for whole-tree token accounting; the `usage` field undercounts as soon as nesting occurs.
findings.ourState: `outputTokens` on the surfaced usage object is taken straight from `msg.usage.output_tokens`, and `inputTokens` from the last non-sidechain assistant message, so both exclude subagent activity. `costUsd` (from `total_cost_usd`) and the `modelUsage` map do include it, and the in-file comment records that the per-message shape is deliberate for context-window display. The result is one usage object mixing a top-level-only token count with a whole-tree cost; whether that reads correctly depends on which field the UI shows next to which.

findings.claim: Cache writes default to a 5-minute TTL under API-key auth, and a named environment variable requests a 1-hour TTL for workloads with gaps between short sessions.
findings.quote: To request a 1-hour TTL on cache writes, set the [`ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H`](/docs/en/env-vars) environment variable.
findings.ourState: `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H` has no reader and no Nessy-side setting; the only `1h` TTL references in the repo are in the interceptor's handling of an Anthropic error string about cache_control block ordering (`unified-network-interceptor.ts:433`). Low impact — a user can export the variable and the SDK subprocess inherits it — but the knob is invisible from the product for a fork whose sessions are typically short and repeated against the same system prompt.

pages.summary: Binds file-change tracking and rewind, a surface Nessy ships as its own `file-checkpoints.ts` + `revertFileCheckpoint`. The tracked-tool set (Write/Edit/NotebookEdit), the symlink / hard-link / non-regular-file skip and its skipped-path count, session scoping and the "directories are not undone" limitation all match. The one divergence is the Claude backend, which never enables the SDK's own checkpoint store.

findings.claim: File checkpointing must be turned on per-session through the SDK option; when it is not, the session performing a rewind has no checkpoint data and the rewind cannot restore anything.
findings.quote: The SDK sets the `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_SDK_FILE_CHECKPOINTING` environment variable internally only when `enable_file_checkpointing` (Python) or `enableFileCheckpointing` (TypeScript) is enabled on the session performing the rewind; the bare CLI never sets it.
findings.ourState: `enableFileCheckpointing` occurs 0 times in `claude-agent.ts` (verified with `grep -ac`, so a NUL byte cannot be hiding it). The SDK query options object built around `claude-agent.ts:1245` passes `cwd`, `includePartialMessages`, `tools`, `permissionMode`, `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions`, `hooks` and the turn-shape options — never `enableFileCheckpointing`. Nessy's own `createFileCheckpoint` has only two non-test callers (Pi's local tool runtime and the Nestor Cloud executor); Claude's Write/Edit/NotebookEdit calls all execute inside the SDK subprocess, so nothing on the Claude path writes a checkpoint.

pages.summary: Mostly container/scaling guidance that does not bind a desktop app, but it restates the SessionStore mirror contract (which `sessions/mirror/` matches, including the three-attempt / timeout-no-retry envelope and the `mirror_error` event) and names one concrete runtime control we have no analogue of.

findings.claim: A background subagent that stops producing output is caught by a stall watchdog, which aborts it, marks the task failed and surfaces the error to the parent with any partial result.
findings.quote: For background subagents only, `CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS` sets a stall watchdog that fires when a `run_in_background` subagent stops producing output; it is not a total-runtime deadline.
findings.ourState: No stall or idle watchdog exists for background subagents. `runBackground`/`runAllAndSeal` is bounded only by the abort signal; there is no output-idle timer.
